provenance.title: Contraceptive initiation practice — reasonable certainty of not being pregnant, and backup contraception
provenance.primarySource: WHO Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR)
provenance.why: MEC answers whether a woman may use a method. It says nothing about when she may start it, whether she needs backup contraception, or for how long. Those are the questions actually asked at the counter, and getting them wrong produces a pregnancy in a woman who believed she was protected.

sourceVerification.note: The SPR text is NOT in docs/reference/who-dak/MANIFEST.json. The Family Planning DAK publishes a data dictionary and vocabulary but no decision logic, so there is no machine-readable artefact to extract these from. This pack was authored against the published recommendations rather than ingested from a pinned artefact, which is a departure from the rule this repository set itself in W1: DAK content is ingested, not paraphrased. It ships as ENGINEERING_SEED for that reason and must not be ratified until the primary text is vendored and each criterion and duration is checked against it line by line. Every rule below names the recommendation it encodes so that check is a comparison, not a rewrite.

criteria.name: No symptoms or signs of pregnancy
criteria.explanation: The checklist below establishes reasonable certainty only in a woman who has no symptoms or signs of pregnancy. This is a gate, not one of the alternatives: meeting a timing criterion does not overrule a positive pregnancy sign.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — how to be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant

adaptation.whoStatement: A health-care provider can be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant if she has no symptoms or signs of pregnancy and meets any one of the listed criteria.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — how to be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant
adaptation.applicablePopulation: Women of reproductive age presenting for contraception

criteria.name: No sexual intercourse since the last normal menses
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 1

adaptation.whoStatement: Has not had sexual intercourse since the last normal menses.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 1

criteria.name: Has been using a reliable contraceptive method correctly and consistently
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 2

adaptation.whoStatement: Has been using a reliable contraceptive method correctly and consistently.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published. Captured as a single clinician judgement rather than derived from the method record, because correct and consistent use is a conversation, not a dispensing history — a woman may hold a valid implant record and a full pill pack she never took.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 2

criteria.name: Within the first 7 days after the start of normal menses
criteria.explanation: daysSinceMensesOnset counts days elapsed, so the day bleeding started is 0 and the seventh day is 6. The off-by-one matters: read the other way it would extend reasonable certainty by a day past what the recommendation allows.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 3

adaptation.whoStatement: Is within the first 7 days after the start of normal menses.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published, with the day count defined as elapsed days from onset so that the boundary is unambiguous at the point of entry.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 3

criteria.name: Within 4 weeks postpartum and not breastfeeding
criteria.explanation: The breastfeeding qualifier is part of the criterion, not decoration. A breastfeeding woman at three weeks postpartum is covered by criterion 6 with its own conditions; she is not covered by this one.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 4

adaptation.whoStatement: Is within 4 weeks postpartum, for non-breastfeeding women.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 4

criteria.name: Within the first 7 days after abortion or miscarriage
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 5

adaptation.whoStatement: Is within the first 7 days post-abortion or miscarriage.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published. The field is worded so it can be answered after any end of pregnancy, however it ended, because post-abortion contraception must be offered without the woman first having to disclose which it was.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 5

criteria.name: Fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic, and less than 6 months postpartum
criteria.explanation: All three conditions together. Any one of them alone is not this criterion, and lactational amenorrhoea with returned menses is not contraception.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 6

adaptation.whoStatement: Is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, amenorrhoeic, and less than 6 months postpartum.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published, with 6 months rendered as 183 days.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — reasonable certainty criterion 6

rules.name: Combined oral contraceptive started within 5 days of menses onset — no backup needed
rules.message: No backup contraception is needed — she is protected from today.
rules.explanation: Started within 5 days of the onset of menses, the combined oral contraceptive is effective immediately.
rules.requiredAction: Give the first pack today and confirm she knows the daily timing. No abstinence or condom period is required.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start combined hormonal contraceptives

adaptation.whoStatement: Combined hormonal contraception started within 5 days of menses onset requires no additional contraceptive protection.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start combined hormonal contraceptives

testCases.name: day 2 of menses needs no backup
day 9 does not take this branch
an unknown cycle day never reaches no-backup

rules.name: Combined oral contraceptive started later than 5 days after menses onset
rules.message: Backup contraception is needed for the next 7 days.
rules.explanation: Started more than 5 days after the onset of menses, the combined oral contraceptive takes 7 days to become reliably effective.
rules.requiredAction: Give the first pack today and supply condoms for 7 days, or advise abstinence for 7 days. Say the number of days out loud — 'use condoms for a week' is what she will remember.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start combined hormonal contraceptives

adaptation.whoStatement: If started more than 5 days after menses onset, additional contraceptive protection is needed for the first 7 days.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published, with condom supply named explicitly in the action so that backup is dispensed rather than only advised.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start combined hormonal contraceptives

testCases.name: day 9 needs 7 days of backup
day 2 does not

rules.name: Combined oral contraceptive with the cycle day not established
rules.message: The date of her last menses is not recorded — advise backup contraception for 7 days.
rules.explanation: Without the cycle day neither the no-backup nor the 7-day branch can be evaluated. Both would stay silent, and a screen showing no backup advice is indistinguishable from one showing that none is needed. Seven days of unnecessary condom use costs nothing; the omission costs a pregnancy.
rules.requiredAction: Supply condoms for 7 days and record the date of her last menstrual period if she can give it.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start combined hormonal contraceptives

adaptation.whoStatement: The recommendation is stated for known cycle timing and does not address the case where the last menstrual period is unknown.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Where the cycle day is not established, treat as requiring the full backup period.
adaptation.rationale: Two complementary rules both evaluate to unknown when the cycle day is missing, so neither fires and the guidance panel renders empty. An empty panel reads as reassurance. The asymmetry of harm is decisive: advising backup that was not needed wastes condoms, omitting backup that was needed produces an unintended pregnancy in a woman who was told she was protected.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start combined hormonal contraceptives

testCases.name: missing cycle day still produces advice
a known cycle day uses the real branch instead

rules.name: Progestogen-only pill started within 5 days of menses onset — no backup needed
rules.message: No backup contraception is needed — she is protected from today.
rules.explanation: Started within 5 days of the onset of menses, the progestogen-only pill is effective immediately.
rules.requiredAction: Give the first pack today and confirm she understands that the progestogen-only pill must be taken at the same time each day.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only pills

adaptation.whoStatement: Progestogen-only pills started within 5 days of menses onset require no additional contraceptive protection.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only pills

testCases.name: day 1 needs no backup
day 10 does not

rules.name: Progestogen-only pill started later than 5 days after menses onset
rules.message: Backup contraception is needed for the next 2 days.
rules.explanation: The progestogen-only pill thickens cervical mucus within about 48 hours, so the backup period is 2 days rather than the 7 required for combined pills.
rules.requiredAction: Give the first pack today and supply condoms for 2 days, or advise abstinence for 2 days.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only pills

adaptation.whoStatement: If started more than 5 days after menses onset, additional contraceptive protection is needed for the first 2 days.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only pills

testCases.name: day 10 needs 2 days of backup
the pill backup period is not the combined one

rules.name: Progestogen-only pill with the cycle day not established
rules.message: The date of her last menses is not recorded — advise backup contraception for 2 days.
rules.explanation: Neither timing branch can be evaluated without the cycle day, and silence would read as no backup being needed.
rules.requiredAction: Supply condoms for 2 days and record the date of her last menstrual period if she can give it.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only pills

adaptation.whoStatement: The recommendation is stated for known cycle timing and does not address an unknown last menstrual period.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Where the cycle day is not established, treat as requiring the full backup period.
adaptation.rationale: Same asymmetry as the combined pill: the cost of unnecessary backup is two days of condoms, the cost of omitted backup is an unintended pregnancy.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only pills

testCases.name: missing cycle day still produces advice

rules.name: Injectable started within 7 days of menses onset — no backup needed
rules.message: No backup contraception is needed — she is protected from today.
rules.explanation: A progestogen-only injectable given within 7 days of the onset of menses is effective immediately.
rules.requiredAction: Give the injection today and book the reinjection date before she leaves.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only injectables

adaptation.whoStatement: Progestogen-only injectables started within 7 days of menses onset require no additional contraceptive protection.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only injectables

testCases.name: DMPA on day 3 needs no backup
the injectable window is wider than the pill window
day 8 does not

rules.name: Injectable started later than 7 days after menses onset
rules.message: Backup contraception is needed for the next 7 days.
rules.explanation: Given more than 7 days after the onset of menses, the injectable takes 7 days to become reliably effective.
rules.requiredAction: Give the injection today, supply condoms for 7 days, and book the reinjection date before she leaves.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only injectables

adaptation.whoStatement: If started more than 7 days after menses onset, additional contraceptive protection is needed for the first 7 days.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only injectables

rules.name: Injectable with the cycle day not established
rules.message: The date of her last menses is not recorded — advise backup contraception for 7 days.
rules.explanation: Neither timing branch can be evaluated without the cycle day, and silence would read as no backup being needed.
rules.requiredAction: Give the injection, supply condoms for 7 days, and record the date of her last menstrual period if she can give it.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only injectables

adaptation.whoStatement: The recommendation is stated for known cycle timing and does not address an unknown last menstrual period.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Where the cycle day is not established, treat as requiring the full backup period.
adaptation.rationale: An injectable is given once and she leaves. There is no second chance to correct the advice before the protection gap has passed.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start progestogen-only injectables

rules.name: Implant or levonorgestrel IUS placed within 7 days of menses onset — no backup needed
rules.message: No backup contraception is needed — she is protected from today.
rules.explanation: An implant or levonorgestrel intrauterine system placed within 7 days of the onset of menses is effective immediately.
rules.requiredAction: Record the insertion date and the removal-due date, and give her something in writing that carries both.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start implants and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system

adaptation.whoStatement: Implants and the LNG-IUD started within 7 days of menses onset require no additional contraceptive protection.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start implants and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system

testCases.name: implant on day 4 needs no backup

rules.name: Implant or levonorgestrel IUS placed later than 7 days after menses onset
rules.message: Backup contraception is needed for the next 7 days.
rules.explanation: Placed more than 7 days after the onset of menses, the implant or levonorgestrel intrauterine system takes 7 days to become reliably effective. The device being in place is not the same as it working.
rules.requiredAction: Supply condoms for 7 days and record the insertion and removal-due dates.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start implants and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system

adaptation.whoStatement: If started more than 7 days after menses onset, additional contraceptive protection is needed for the first 7 days.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published, with the explanation stating plainly that a placed device is not yet an effective one — the visible procedure is what a woman will take as the moment protection began.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start implants and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system

testCases.name: IUS on day 15 needs 7 days of backup

rules.name: Implant or levonorgestrel IUS with the cycle day not established
rules.message: The date of her last menses is not recorded — advise backup contraception for 7 days.
rules.explanation: Neither timing branch can be evaluated without the cycle day, and silence would read as no backup being needed.
rules.requiredAction: Supply condoms for 7 days and record the date of her last menstrual period if she can give it.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start implants and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system

adaptation.whoStatement: The recommendation is stated for known cycle timing and does not address an unknown last menstrual period.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Where the cycle day is not established, treat as requiring the full backup period.
adaptation.rationale: A woman who has just had a device inserted is the least likely of all to believe she needs condoms. The advice has to be given explicitly or it will not be inferred.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start implants and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system

testCases.name: missing cycle day still produces advice

rules.name: Copper intrauterine device — effective immediately, no backup at any point in the cycle
rules.message: No backup contraception is needed — the copper device is effective from insertion.
rules.explanation: The copper intrauterine device works on contact and is effective immediately regardless of where she is in her cycle. It is the only method here with no backup period at all, which is also why it is the emergency contraceptive of choice.
rules.requiredAction: Record the insertion date and the removal-due date, and teach her to check the threads.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start the copper-bearing intrauterine device

adaptation.whoStatement: The copper-bearing IUD is effective immediately and requires no additional contraceptive protection.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published. Deliberately written without a cycle-day condition rather than with one that is always satisfied, so that a missing last menstrual period cannot make this rule silent.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start the copper-bearing intrauterine device

testCases.name: copper IUD needs no backup on any day
copper IUD needs no backup with the cycle day unknown either

rules.name: Pregnancy could not be excluded — do not deny contraception for it
rules.message: Pregnancy cannot be excluded today. This is not a reason to send her away without a method.
rules.explanation: Reasonable certainty could not be established from the checklist. A pregnancy test settles it where one is available, but the absence of a test is a supply problem, not a clinical contraindication — turning her away carries its own risk of the pregnancy she came to prevent.
rules.requiredAction: Offer a pregnancy test if one is available. If it is not, a short-acting hormonal method may still be started today with backup contraception and a return visit; do not defer her on the test alone.
rules.monitoringInstruction: Ask her to return if her next expected menses does not come.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — how to be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant

adaptation.whoStatement: A woman should not be denied a contraceptive method solely because a pregnancy test is unavailable.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Adopted as published, and surfaced as an explicit alert rather than as background guidance.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — how to be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant

testCases.name: unresolved certainty raises the safeguard
established certainty does not

rules.name: Defer intrauterine insertion until pregnancy is excluded
rules.message: Do not insert an intrauterine device today — pregnancy has not been excluded.
rules.explanation: This qualifies the safeguard above rather than contradicting it. She should not be sent away, but insertion into a pregnant uterus is the one initiation that cannot be undone by stopping the method, and pregnancy is a category 4 for intrauterine devices. The device is deferred; contraception is not.
rules.requiredAction: Start a short-acting method today as a bridge, give her a return date for insertion, and record the plan so the next clinician knows an insertion is owed rather than declined.
sourceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start the copper-bearing intrauterine device
WHO MEC — pregnancy, intrauterine devices

adaptation.whoStatement: Intrauterine devices should not be inserted when the woman is pregnant; insertion requires reasonable certainty that she is not.
adaptation.nationalStatement: Where reasonable certainty is not established, defer insertion, start a bridging method the same day, and record the deferred insertion as owed.
adaptation.rationale: The do-not-deny safeguard is correct and, standing alone next to an intrauterine method, reads as permission to insert. Naming the bridging method and the return date turns a deferral into a plan; without them a deferral is a refusal with a softer word, and she does not come back.
evidenceRefs: WHO SPR — when to start the copper-bearing intrauterine device
WHO MEC — pregnancy, intrauterine devices

testCases.name: IUD insertion is deferred when pregnancy is not excluded
an implant is not deferred
established certainty allows insertion
